The blackeye goby Rhinogobiops nicholsii is a small-bodied, nest-guarding teleost that inhabits rocky reef environments along the eastern Pacific coast, where it exhibits a life history tightly coupled to stable thermal conditions. Comparative studies of this species have documented that during early development, embryos and newly hatched larvae are particularly sensitive to ambient temperature, with most experimental work conducted at a water temperature of 9.8 °C [T = 9.8 °C]. Under these controlled thermal conditions, hatching from the fertilised, yolk-laden egg occurs after just 4 days [ab = 4 days], a remarkably rapid embryogenesis that likely reflects an adaptation to the cool, productive waters of the California Current system at a temperature of 9.8 °C [T = 9.8 °C]. The resulting yolk-sac larva emerges at a very small size, with the wet weight at birth being only 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a lecithotrophic mass that must sustain the larva through the critical transition to first exogenous feeding. This initial mass, derived from an egg diameter of about 0.7 millimeters, is among the lowest recorded for a temperate goby and underscores the species reliance on abundant planktonic prey immediately following yolk absorption.

Sexual maturation in Rhinogobiops nicholsii occurs at markedly different body sizes between the sexes, a pattern that has been confirmed across several populations examined in field surveys from central Baja California to Monterey Bay. Females attain puberty, defined here as the onset of vitellogenesis and the ability to produce mature oocytes, when they reach a total length at puberty of 4.7 centimeters [Lp = 4.7 centimeters]. Males, in contrast, require a larger body dimension before reproductive activation and the onset of spermiation; the total length at puberty for males is 7.2 centimeters [Lp = 7.2 centimeters]. This sexual dimorphism in size at maturity is a common feature among nest-guarding gobies and is often interpreted as a consequence of intrasexual competition among males for access to breeding sites and receptive females. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, the somatic mass at which the HPG axis becomes fully operational, has been measured at approximately 1.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.1 grams] for newly matured individuals of both sexes, though larger males typically dominate spawning territories.

As individuals continue to grow beyond the pubertal stage, the divergence in ultimate size between the sexes becomes even more pronounced. The ultimate total length for females, the maximum standard length that female blackeye gobies can achieve in the wild, has been documented at 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a value that places this species among the larger-bodied gobies of the eastern Pacific. Although males can also approach this length, the ultimate wet weight reached by large adults, estimated from length-weight regressions, is approximately 36.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 36.4 grams] for fully grown, reproductively active individuals. This mass is consistent with a robust, benthic-feeding fish that occupies a territory and engages in prolonged parental care of the demersal egg mass. Growth rates in this species appear to slow considerably after the first year, with most individuals reaching close to their asymptotic size within 2 to 3 years, after which energy is increasingly channeled into reproductive effort rather than somatic mass accumulation.

Reproductive output in Rhinogobiops nicholsii has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic the natural thermal regime of the species habitat. At a constant water temperature of 9.8 °C [T = 9.8 °C], females produce demersal, adhesive eggs in multiple clutches over the course of an extended spawning season. The maximum reproductive rate, when decomposed, reveals that females deposit clutches containing roughly 4788 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 4788 eggs per spawning event] and are capable of approximately 5 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 5 spawning events per year]. This high fecundity, combined with the devoted nest-guarding behavior of the male, results in a recruitment strategy that can sustain local populations even under considerable predation pressure from sculpins and other reef-associated predators.

Longevity in this species is modest but typical for a small, warm-temperate goby, with natural mortality occurring primarily through predation and senescence rather than catastrophic environmental events. The maximum recorded lifespan for Rhinogobiops nicholsii, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimations conducted at a mean water temperature of 9.8 °C [T = 9.8 °C], is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This lifespan places the blackeye goby among the longer-lived members of the Gobiidae, many of which have annual or biennial life cycles. The extended juvenile period, during which individuals must acquire a territory and reach the necessary size threshold for reproduction, likely contributes to this comparatively slow life history pace. Together with the rapid embryogenesis, pronounced sexual size dimorphism at maturity, and high fecundity, these life history traits paint a picture of a species that is well-adapted to the relatively stable, cool upwelling zones it inhabits along the Pacific coast.
